history.content: My sorghum plants stay short and yellow even though the rains are good, what is happening?

Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot.

history.content: How can I control Striga witchweed on my sorghum field?

draws.answer: Striga, the flowering weed of Sorghum striga, must be controlled before the sorghum flower buds. First, sow a sorghum variety that matures in 55-75 days and plant your seeds between November and March in areas where sorghum is grown year after year. Two weeks after sowing, perform the first weeding to keep the field clean. Then, at 30-35 days after sowing, apply the top-dress urea at 150-200 kg per hectare, and repeat the urea application at 100 kg per hectare when the sorghum reaches panicle initiation, which is roughly 40-50 days after sowing. Include a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the rotation and cut the sorghum stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing root nodules remain in the soil. If you need variety selection advice or the exact timing of striga control, see ICAT.

Striga witchweed must be removed before the sorghum flower buds appear. history.content: What is Cassava brown streak virus and how can I manage it?

draws.answer: Cassava brown streak virus is the disease it is named for, and it makes leaves turn yellow and turn brown from the bottom up with no spots or streaks. First, uproot and destroy the strongly affected plants because they spread the virus. Then, for the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and avoid any that have the yellow or dark streaks. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. No spray can cure an infected plant. For the next planting, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy, with normal green leaves and no distortion. history.content: My sorghum looks stunted and yellow, and I see a pink flowered weed near the stem, what should I do?

draws.answer: Those signs point to striga in your sorghum crop. Plant a striga tolerant sorghum variety and cross it with grain sorghum to obtain a grain sorghum variety that also tolerates striga. The problem is thrips, pod borers and aphids attacking your sorghum. Sow a sorghum variety that matures in 55 to 75 days and plant it when the rains are strong, usually from mid-June to early July. When you reach flowering, about 30-35 days after sowing, pull out the Striga plant and any weeds that may have emerged. If you see a second maize crop in the same field next year, widen the spacing between the pockets. I cannot give you any other specific measure because it depends on the variety you are using.

history.content: There is a purple weed around my sorghum roots and the plants stay dwarf even with rain, any advice?

history.content: My cassava leaves have yellow blotches along the veins, what should I do?

draws.answer: It is cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy the cassava plants that are strongly mottled and stunted. When you plant again, take cuttings only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation. Do not cut from any plant that shows yellow mottling, twisted or shrunken leaves. Use an improved tolerant variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, you should go to ITRA.

Then, for the next planting, cut only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. history.content: My ewes are coughing, have runny eyes and noses, and some have died within a day, what is happening?

draws.answer: The signs you describe are typical of tick-borne disease, the parasite *Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus*. Contact with ticks carrying the parasite can spread the disease, so avoid grazing the affected animals in the same area where others are well. Hand-pick all visible ticks on every animal in the herd, not only the ill ones. Call the veterinary service the same day for diagnosis and the correct drug and dose. Inform the vet of the urine colour, because red to black requires a specific treatment. Do not reuse needles between animals. The veterinary service will provide the appropriate medication.

You are dealing with a tick-borne disease in your sheep. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify whether it is gall sickness or redwater and provide the correct drug and dose. When you speak to the vet, describe the colour of the urine because red to black indicates redwater and yellow-brown without red indicates gall sickness. Keep the sick sheep in shade, give them clean water, and avoid making them walk because they are short of red blood cells. Hand-pick any ticks you see on all the sheep, not just the sick one, to prevent further spread. The veterinary service will give you the appropriate medication.

Then burn or bury any dead goats in a safe place and do not move or sell any animal. After this, vaccinate the whole herd against gall sickness. The disease spreads through direct contact, soil and water, and contaminated feed or water. Contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately.

If the animals keep refusing food or you see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, see the veterinary service.

history.content: I see a purple flowered weed clinging around the base of my sorghum plants that are short. What should I do?

draws.answer: The purple-flowered Striga, known locally as the striga plant, is the parasitic weed of sorghum that causes the stunting. Pull the striga plants out before they flower, using a weeding method that stops the striga from flowering. Then sow your sorghum early and use the recommended close spacing. Protect the sorghum during the flowering stage to keep the striga from stealing nutrients. For further advice on striga control or to see a tolerant sorghum variety, go to ICAT.

At 2-3 weeks after sowing, perform the first weeding to keep the field clean. When the plants reach panicle initiation, pull out the purple-striped Striga before they flower. Keep the field area weeded and, if you see any angular water-soaked spots with wilting instead of leaf deformation, visit ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.

history.content: My herd has sudden diarrhoea and many goats are dying quickly, almost all of them. What is happening?

draws.answer: This is a case of trypanosomiasis, called nagana in local terminology, transmitted by tsetse flies. First, report the problem to the veterinary service so they can confirm the disease and prescribe the right trypanocide. Do not try to treat yourself. Then stop grazing in riverine bush where the flies are active, especially during biting hours, and consider fly control. Keep the animals well fed and watered to help them cope. history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga is the plant that grows between the roots of sorghum and pulls the seedling out. First, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. At two to three weeks thin the seedlings to two or three plants per pocket and perform the first weeding without breaking the ridges. After weeding, apply the three flowering-stage sprays to protect the pods. For a variety that matches your region and season, see ICAT.

Striga, also called groundsel, is the parasite that climbs sorghum plants and takes their stem, so a stalk taken out by the weed becomes its host. First, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five grains per pocket at a depth of three to five centimetres and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Ten days after sowing, spread NPK 15-15-15 on the low-land zone at 200 kilograms per hectare in a pocket, and repeat the dose as the crop grows. Keep the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. When the two-row sorghum reaches panicle initiation, about 30 to 35 days after sowing, apply Urea, at 150 kilograms per hectare. No spray will remove Striga. For help matching a variety and exact rates, visit ICAT.
